items.title: Offutt’s Newest K9 Team is Mission-Ready
items.author: Dana Heard
items.summary: When Staff Sgt. Michael Pita unlatched the kennel gate last December to meet his new partner, he was not expecting to get a full-body embrace.
items.body: When Staff Sgt. Michael Pita unlatched the kennel gate last December to meet his new partner, he was not expecting to get a full-body embrace. Hector, an energetic Belgian Malinois, stood up on his hind legs, placing his front paws against Pita’s chest. At 5-foot-10, Pita found himself nearly eye-to-eye with a dog standing up to his chin, with his tail wagging, showing his eagerness to work. That enthusiasm was the beginning of a transformative journey for both the 55th Security Forces Squadron handler and Offutt’s newest military working dog. The Department of War’s MWD program, managed by the 341st Training Squadron at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, produces all U.S. military detection dogs throughout the world. When a canine arrives at its first duty station, they are matched with a handler to establish a partnership from the ground up. Pita and Hector spent their entire first week together avoiding rigid restrictions. Through a method known as inducive training, the pair focused solely on long walks, playing, and unstructured bonding. “During that time, it was all about seeing what behaviors he offers naturally and making our one-on-one time valuable,” Pita explained. “You learn what motivates him, what techniques work best when teaching a new task, and how to approach obstacles we might encounter in the field.” When Hector arrived, he was comfortable sweeping enclosed environments such as barracks, warehouses, and vehicle bays. However, he was not as comfortable in open fields and roadways. Outside the confines of four walls, wind patterns and open terrain required a different type of drive and focus that needed to be cultivated to succeed. Pita dedicated weeks to showing Hector the value of working in open areas. Through patience and tailored reinforcement, Hector learned to effectively read open-air scent cones; the invisible, funnel-shaped plumes of odor carried by the wind. Today, Hector sweeps wide roadway perimeters and open fields with the same precision he displays indoors. “In regard to Hector, I would say his progress has been spectacular; he is one of the best dogs Offutt has seen in the last eight years,” said Staff Sgt. Keaton Leshko, 55th SFS MWD trainer. “He is top of the line in his work and continues to improve every day.” Hector’s development took another step forward during his patrol training. Arriving as a single-purpose detection dog, Hector had never learned controlled aggression or bite work. Pita took on the challenge of building that capability from scratch. To teach Hector the nuances of controlled aggression, Pita often stepped into the heavy bite suit himself for ‘self-decoying.’ By taking on the impacts directly Pita was able to teach Hector exactly how to turn his aggression on and off on command. “Being able to train his bite work from the ground up and showcase his new capability, I was proud to say, ‘I did that!’” Pita said. That discipline was on full display during a recent demonstration for the West Virginia Mountaineers baseball team during their College World Series tour of Offutt. Spectators watched Hector execute the ‘escort’ command; walking calmly alongside a simulated suspect without biting. “In the field, we might be by ourselves while backup is still on the way,” Pita noted. “We instill the escort command, so the MWD assists us in moving suspects safely back to our patrol vehicle after an apprehension.” With detection certification completed in March 2026 and full patrol qualification secured in July 2026, the team now stands fully mission-ready for installation security and explosive detection. “Staff Sgt. Pita has a great work ethic and sacrificed a lot of time and effort to get Hector to where he is today,” said Tech. Sgt. Brenden Smith, 55th SFS kennel master. “They have been one of the best military working dog teams I’ve worked with since arriving at Offutt.” For Pita and Hector, the long hours in the bite suit and the early morning sweeps are simply what it takes to protect the base. For Pita, it all traces back to that first moment at the kennel door; the chin-high greeting that grew into a partnership.

items.title: PCU John F. Kennedy Welcomes New Chiefs and Carries Legacy of Leadership
items.author: SN Roberto Oropeza
items.summary: Pre-Commissioning Unit (PCU) John F. Kennedy (CVN 79) pinned 29 1st Class Petty Officers to Chief Petty Officer during a ceremony.
items.body:
JOINT EXPEDITIONARY BASE LITTLE CREEK, Va. — At Gator Theater on board Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek-Fort Eustis, Pre-Commissioning Unit John F. Kennedy (CVN 79) pinned 29 1st Class Petty Officers to Chief Petty Officer during a ceremony with crew members, command leaders, family and friends in attendance, September 17, 2026. Congratulations to our newest Chiefs! Stand on business!

For the new Chiefs, the ceremony represented more than an advancement. It marked the beginning of a chapter not defined by a new title or gold insignia, but greater responsibility, higher expectations and a commitment to developing the Sailors entrusted to their leadership. Chief Aviation Electronics Technician Christopher Torres, assigned to Engineering Department, shared his first takeaways from the ceremony.

“The feeling of having these anchors is great,” said Torres. This is something I have worked towards for a long time, and it was the result of a combination of people believing in me and me doing the work. The six weeks of initiation Chief had its ups and downs for sure and you may not understand it all at first, but it was definitely rewarding.”

Established April 1, 1893, the Chief Petty Officer rank has long represented technical expertise, deckplate leadership and mentorship. Chiefs connect the Navy’s officer and enlisted ranks while upholding the standards necessary to maintain an effective fighting force.

Chiefs must set an example to help Sailors understand what right looks like, correct deficiencies, recognize achievement, and provide guidance for professional and personal growth. They must also maintain an environment in which Sailors are treated with dignity and respect while also being held accountable for their actions when necessary. The new Chiefs aboard John F. Kennedy inherited this legacy and responsibility as the ship prepares for fleet operations. The standards they establish today will influence the Sailors who will take the ship to sea, operate its systems and carry out its missions around the world. John F Kennedy’s Commanding Officer, Captain Doug Langenberg, congratulated the Chiefs and pointed towards their new standards and practices for the ship.

“The Navy does not expect you to merely preserve what they handed you - [the U.S. Navy] expects you to strengthen it, to improve it, to add your mark, so that when your time is done, your Navy is better than when you found it,” said Langenberg. “This is the infinite responsibility of the Chief Petty Officer: to lead in such a way that Sailors who come after you will inherit not only the same Navy, but a stronger, more resilient one…To our newest Chiefs, congratulations.”

Chiefs do not carry those responsibilities alone. The Chiefs Mess brings together leaders with different experiences and perspectives to identify challenges, develop solutions and support the command’s mission. Its strength comes from a collective willingness to share lessons, support one another and place the crew’s needs above personal interests. By observing performance, teaching technical skills and encouraging professional development, Chiefs help Sailors become confident members of a cohesive crew. They reinforce watchstanding standards, promote readiness and show Sailors how their duties contribute to the ship’s mission.

Chief Aviation Boatswain’s Mate (Handling) Braxton James, assigned to Air Department, shared a crucial skill in understanding how he has learned to lead.

“A big thing I learned from the Chief initiation is to ask for help,” said James. “Sometimes we get caught up in thinking we can do everything ourselves and that is going to lead to the accolades that we want. You have to realize that along the way you needed help. Even if you didn’t ask for it, you always have help. It is not a weakness to ask for it.”

That responsibility to help is especially important aboard John F. Kennedy as its Sailors establish the foundation for future Sailors that will operate the world’s most advanced aircraft carrier.

The Chiefs who lead those Sailors have an opportunity to shape individual careers as well as the future of the ship’s culture. Welcoming new members strengthens the John F. Kennedy’s Chiefs Mess by adding their skills and perspectives to its collective experience. The new Chiefs’ success will be measured not only by their accomplishments, but also by the Sailors they develop, the teams they strengthen and the examples they set.

John F Kennedy’s Command Master Chief Craig Johnson communicated a call to action for the ship’s newest Chief Petty Officers.

“It is going to take the Chief to inspire these Sailors - to make sure that we are doing the right thing,” said Johnson. “We are going to maintain the standards, enforce standards, and are going to own our professional and personal development and that of the Sailors we are charged to lead.”

The pinning ceremony served as a reminder that the Navy’s strength depends on its people and the leaders who prepare them to serve. As John F. Kennedy continues its transition toward fleet operations, its newest Chiefs will help shape the ship’s culture, strengthen its crew and prepare Sailors for the challenges of operating at sea.

items.title: U.S., Canadian Forces to Rehearse Joint Maritime Strikes in the Bering Sea
items.author: Alaskan Command Public Affairs
items.summary: U.S. and Canadian forces will conduct joint maneuvers in the Bering Sea, Sept. 18-22, approximately 100 nautical miles north of Dutch Harbor, under the command and control of U.S. Northern Command and Alaskan Command’s Operation TUNDRA MERLIN.
items.body:
BERING SEA, Alaska— U.S. and Canadian forces will conduct joint maneuvers in the Bering Sea, Sept. 18-22, approximately 100 nautical miles north of Dutch Harbor, under the command and control of U.S. Northern Command and Alaskan Command’s Operation TUNDRA MERLIN.

The operation will integrate U.S. Coast Guard and Royal Canadian Navy surface and subsurface vessels. There will also be a mix of Royal Canadian Air Force Maritime Patrol and Reconnaissance Aircraft and Alaska-based United States Air Force F-35 fighter and E-3 Airborne Warning and Control System aircraft to enable multi-domain operations.

During the operation, the binational forces will execute multiple simulated maritime target engagements. Validating targeting information flow and exercising engagement processes increases joint force capabilities to defeat threats to the homelands.

“Our ability to detect activity, make timely decisions, and position forces where they are needed gives a potential adversary reason to reconsider aggression,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force. “Every TUNDRA MERLIN event prepares the force to fight and win in the Arctic, strengthens command and control, and improves our ability to operate seamlessly across services and nations, reinforcing the credibility of our collective defense.”

Operation TUNDRA MERLIN integrates forces assigned to NORAD and USNORTHCOM with US allies and mission partners to deter potential threats to the homelands in the Alaskan Theater of Operations.

items.title: Lost at Pearl Harbor, WWII Soldier Will Be Laid to Rest Close to Home in Maryland
items.author: Daniela Vestal
items.summary: FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Pfc. Owen M. Norris, missing from World War II, will be interred Sept. 26 at West Liberty United Methodist Church Cemetery in Marriottsville, Maryland. Services and interment are being coordinated by Vaughn Greene Funeral Services.
items.body:
FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Pfc. Owen M. Norris, missing from World War II, will be interred Sept. 26 at West Liberty United Methodist Church Cemetery in Marriottsville, Maryland. Services and interment are being coordinated by Vaughn Greene Funeral Services.

Norris entered the service from Maryland and was a member of the 29th Chemical Decontamination Company.

On May 21, 1944, American personnel were loading ammunition and fuel onto ships moored in West Loch, Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, when an explosion erupted on the landing ship LST 353.

The blast sent flaming debris onto a group of adjacent ships. More than one hundred Americans lost their lives in the incident, and massive fires burned for around 24 hours, hampering rescue and recovery efforts. Norris was killed in the disaster. Despite a search for survivors in the immediate aftermath, his remains were not identified.

Between May and June 1944, U.S. forces buried 47 sets of remains from the disaster whose identity could not be ascertained at the Halawa Naval Cemetery. These remains were later interred as Unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. In November 2024, Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency personnel exhumed one of these sets of remains, designated X-286, and accessioned them into the DPAA laboratory for analysis.

There, scientists used modern forensic techniques to identify Norris.

DPAA accounted for Norris on July 7, 2026.

U.S. Army Human Resources Command’s Past Conflict Repatriations Branch plays a vital role in the process of identifying, locating and contacting subsequent generation family members of Soldiers missing or killed in action during WWII and the Korean War to positively identify previously undiscovered or unknown remains.

Media interested in covering and/or obtaining more information about the funeral and interment should contact Vaughn Greene Funeral Services, 410-655-0015.

items.title: Antiterrorism Awareness Month: Our Shared Responsibility
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: It has been 25 years since our nation felt the pain and fear of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. I can remember everything about those moments. I had the TV on as I was getting ready to leave. I watched as reporters filmed the fire on the first tower. I watched as the second plane struck the tower. It felt like the world had stopped. I couldn’t believe what I was seeing, and I felt like I had to make myself breathe.
items.body:
It has been 25 years since our nation felt the pain and fear of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. I can remember everything about those moments. I had the TV on as I was getting ready to leave. I watched as reporters filmed the fire on the first tower. I watched as the second plane struck the tower. It felt like the world had stopped. I couldn’t believe what I was seeing, and I felt like I had to make myself breathe.

Since that day, our nation has continued to adapt to an ever-changing world of threats. In advance of this anniversary, we observe Antiterrorism Awareness Month (ATAM) throughout August. Daily Tasking Order (DTO) 26-07-09 directs us as follows:

“USACE will execute the Army’s Annual Antiterrorism Awareness Month (ATAM) throughout August 2026, delegating execution authority to commanders and directors at all echelons. The strategic objective is to institutionalize heightened antiterrorism awareness and vigilance enterprise-wide, thereby mitigating the risk of terrorist attacks and safeguarding USACE personnel, critical infrastructure, and resources from violent extremist threats. During the month of August USACE conducts comprehensive Antiterrorism (AT) education and awareness operations targeting Soldiers, Department of the Army (DA) Civilians, contractors, and family members in order to instill heightened organizational vigilance, deter terrorist activities, and protect critical personnel and resources.”

As we approach the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, this year’s campaign reinforces our resolve. By promoting focused ATAM themes, we will sustain a proactive defensive posture designed to enhance situational awareness and organizational vigilance across the District.

What does this mean for our district?

Headquarters sets the strategy, but the actual work of protecting our people happens right here, every day. A strong security culture means safety is not just the responsibility of the Antiterrorism Officer (ATO) or the guards at the door — it is a shared responsibility.

The events of 25 years ago showed us the worst of what can happen when our adversaries succeed. This August, let’s honor that memory by looking out for one another, remaining vigilant and ensuring our District remains a hard target.

Stay safe, and thank you for doing your part.

How USACE Headquarters guidance is being implemented at the Rock Island District:

• Go Beyond the Checkbox: We all must complete our mandatory Level I AT Awareness Training, but true security requires more than basic compliance. We need to apply these concepts every day. Be situationally aware, don’t allow tailgating through secure doors, remove your CAC when leaving your desk, and practice good operational security (OPSEC) in public spaces. • See Something, Say Something: Threat recognition is our collective defense against violent extremism and insider threats. Familiarize yourself with reporting systems such as iWATCH Army and iSalute. If you observe suspicious activity — such as unauthorized photography of our facilities, unusual questions about our operations or concerning behavioral changes in a colleague — report it immediately. • Enhance Our Survivability: Take time this month to review your office’s emergency action plans. Familiarize yourself with primary and secondary evacuation routes, and mentally rehearse your active shooter response procedures. Preparedness saves lives. • Trust the Process: While you remain vigilant, know that District leadership and our ATOs are working hard behind the scenes. They are actively reviewing facility-level plans, conducting Random Antiterrorism Measures (RAMs) and tailoring Force Protection Condition (FPCON) measures to ensure our environment remains secure.

items.title: Air Force Set Up a Depot in UK During Epic Fury for Faster Battle Repairs
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: Air Force depots are not typically meant for quick repair jobs, but during Operation Epic Fury, the service moved some of its stateside heavy maintenance capability forward to fix battle-damaged aircraft closer to the fight. The post Air Force Set Up a Depot in UK During Epic Fury for Faster Battle Repairs appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —Air Force depots are not typically meant for quick repair jobs—aircraft can stay in depot for weeks and months getting repairs—but during Operation Epic Fury, the service moved some of its stateside heavy maintenance capability forward to fix battle-damaged aircraft closer to the fight.

As the war with Iran stretched from its projected timeline of weeks into several months, Air Force leaders were forced to adapt its aircraft maintenance strategy for a prolonged conflict.

The service relies on three maintenance depots at Hill Air Force Base, Utah; Robins Air Force Base, Ga.; and Tinker Air Force Base, Okla.—to conduct major maintenance overhauls and inspections on fighters, bombers, airlifters, and other aircraft.

During Epic Fury, barrages of Iranian missile and drone attacks on U.S. forces operating out of Middle East resulted in levels of battle damage that normally would have required the aircraft to be transported back stateside for repairs.

Instead, Air Force Materiel Command temporarily surged a depot capability to RAF Mildenhall in the United Kingdom so damaged aircraft could be patched up and sent back into combat, AFMC Commander Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry told an audience this week at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber conference .

“Most people think of depots as Tinker, Robbins, and Hill; well, it doesn’t need to be just there,” Hurry said. “We knew you needed a capability out at Mildenhall … what if we push that forward?”

“That’s what we’ve been asking all of our Airmen—how do we do things smarter? How do we deliver capability faster? It doesn’t have to be 7,000 miles away.”

Air Mobility Command’s new boss, Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, said Hurry’s move paid off, describing how the depot operation quickly repaired damaged aerial refueling booms on KC-135 Stratotanker s.

“I think we turned 30 [booms] instead of bringing them all the way back to the states,” Tulley said, adding it was a great example of “generating readiness in contact.”

Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink and Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach made readiness a defining priority soon after taking their jobs last year. The intense pace of operations against Iran will stress that focus, with much of the fleet likely to need heavy maintenance overhauls to reset.

The Air Force’s proposed 2027 budget includes $4.2 billion for the Consolidated Sustainment Activity Group, which is responsible for managing spare parts.

“We absolutely need additional funding for spares,” Hurry said, adding “right now , we have a $14 billion hole in supply.”

“I know we’re not going to get it all at once, … but once we get even a penny, we have to be ready to execute it,” Hurry said. That will mean securing long-term contracts to inject stability into the supply chain.

“The other thing is, we’re looking for is multiple sources of supply; gone are the days of monopolies. We can’t just have one person producing the one critical part,” Hurry said. “I need five of you producing them because if we get down to the crunch, we’re going to have to have a healthy shelf so that we can fight globally.”

Meanwhile, Hurry said AFMC has started using artificial intelligence tools to improve forecasting accuracy. “We’re using all sorts of things to try to make sure we better understand where the needs are and where we can position those critical assets globally around the world,” she said.

Additive manufacturing is another tool AFMC has started to use to “reverse engineer some of the parts that we need,” she added.

But technology alone isn’t enough, she said, adding that “process improvement” can solve a lot of challenges.

“Quite frankly, if we can understand the process and break it down into constraint and mitigate that constrain, the collective throughput of the entire system goes so much better,” Hurry said. “That’s exactly what’s going on in the depot. That’s exactly what we did when we surged operations for [Epic Fury].”

The 55th Wing officially retired the EC-130H Compass Call aircraft in a ceremony Sept. 18 at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz., while the 355th Wing there retired its final A-10 Warthog, another major transition for the base.

More than 130 Airmen and Guardians have returned to service after leaving the military rather than receive the COVID-19 vaccine. And more could follow, an Air Force official said.

As the threat of Iranian-made drones grew, the Air Force rushed last year to equip F-15E Strike Eagles in the Middle East with a cheap, cost-effective way of defeating them. The service fielded the new capability in roughly a week.

Sept. 17, 2026

An F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing crashed during a training mission in Michigan on Sept. 17. The fighter's sole pilot ejected and is in stable condition at a local hospital.

When Space Force leaders started talking about expanding the service early this year, the idea was simple: double the size of the force in the next five years. At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, officials detailed just how they’re planning to grow so much so quickly.

The Air Force’s new Collaborative Combat Aircraft will take part in their first large-force engagement exercise in December, the head of the drones’ Experimental Operations Unit said Sept. 15.

The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters.

As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.

Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.

items.title: Lost in 1950, Korean War Soldier to be Laid to Rest in Michigan
items.author: Daniela Vestal
items.summary: FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Cpl. Vester Hicks, Jr. 17, who was killed during the Korean War, will be interred Sept. 25, at Great Lakes National Cemetery in Holly, Michigan. Services and interment are being coordinated by Czopek Funeral Home.
items.body: FORT KNOX, Ky. – The remains of U.S. Army Cpl. Vester Hicks, Jr. 17, who was killed during the Korean War, will be interred Sept. 25, at Great Lakes National Cemetery in Holly, Michigan. Services and interment are being coordinated by Czopek Funeral Home. Hicks entered the Army from Tennessee and served in C Company, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division. On the evening of Nov. 27, 1950, Chinese Communist Forces launched a massive attack against U.S. and United Nations troops positioned around the Chosin Reservoir in northeast North Korea. Elements of the 31st and 32nd Infantry Regiments were defending ground north of Sinhung-ni on the east side of the reservoir when the numerically superior enemy forced a withdrawal toward Hagaru-ri on Dec. 1. The route south, cut by Chinese roadblocks and subjected to constant fire from surrounding high ground, broke the column into smaller groups that were attacked repeatedly during the fighting withdrawal. Many soldiers were killed or captured, and survivors reached friendly lines at Hagaru-ri on Dec. 2 and 3. Hicks went missing during this withdrawal on or about Dec. 2, but the specific circumstances of his loss are unknown. In 1954, during Operation Glory, North Korea returned remains believed to be those of American service members, including one set designated Unknown X-15894. These remains, reportedly recovered from the east side of the Chosin Reservoir, were buried at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu. On March 8, 2021, as part of Phase Four of the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency’s Korean War Disinterment Project, X-15894 was disinterred and accessioned into a DPAA Laboratory for analysis. There, scientists used modern forensic techniques to identify Hicks. DPAA accounted for Hicks on Sept. 4, 2025. For more information on DPAA’s efforts to locate and identify Hicks, please visit: https://www.dpaa.mil/News-Stories/ID-Announcements/Article/4322575/soldier-accounted-for-from-korean-war-hicks-jr-v/ U.S. Army Human Resources Command’s Past Conflict Repatriations Branch plays a vital role in the process of identifying, locating and contacting subsequent generation family members of Soldiers missing or killed in action during WWII and the Korean War to positively identify previously undiscovered or unknown remains. items.title: The Adventures of Spencer Kellogg Brown (25 SEP 1863)
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: On Sept. 25, 1863, a Union sailor, Spencer Kellogg Brown, was taken to the gallows in Richmond, Virginia, to hang for two offenses: being a spy for the Union and a deserter from the Confederate army. The young man’s life had been rife with unusual adventures along the way.
items.body: On Sept. 25, 1863, a Union sailor, Spencer Kellogg Brown, was taken to the gallows in Richmond, Virginia, to hang for two offenses: being a spy for the Union and a deserter from the Confederate army. The young man’s life had been rife with unusual adventures along the way. In 1854, staunch abolitionist Orville Brown moved his family from New York to found the town of Osawatomie, Kansas. Two years later, he watched his house burn during a raid by pro-slavery bandits aimed at punishing the radical abolitionist John Brown, who had also moved to the town. Although the two Brown families were unrelated, Orville’s 14-year-old son Spencer—Spense to his family—was mistaken for John Brown’s son, captured, and held prisoner for many weeks. Because the name Brown was hated in the region for years afterwards, in January 1861, Spencer fled to Kentucky to enlist in the U.S. Army as Spencer Kellogg. Transferred to St. Louis to guard the Union armory, in mid-June, Spencer found himself in command of a group of mounted scouts patrolling throughout Missouri and peppered his brother (still in Kansas) with questions about the numbers and whereabouts of Southern sympathizers. An impressed Maj. Gen. John Frémont, then commander of the Western Department, discharged the enlisted Spencer and appointed him a first lieutenant to recruit and form the “Lyon Legion” scout unit of the 12th Regiment, Missouri Volunteers. Sadly, when Frémont was removed from command, Spencer’s commission was voided, so he enlisted in the U.S. Navy and was assigned to the U.S.S. Essex gunboat under the command of Capt. (later Commodore) William D. Porter on the Mississippi River. Having enjoyed his previous scouting experiences, in January 1862, Spencer devised a plan to reconnoiter the Confederate batteries along the river. Approved by Captain Porter, Spencer and a fellow sailor, known to history only as Trussel, “deserted” for what was to be a ten-day “secret expedition.” Over the next two months, Spencer traveled the length of the river as a Union “deserter” attached to Confederate forces. As he helped their engineers with survey work, he made notes and maps of Confederate fortifications, breastworks, guns, and troop strengths. In Tennessee in early April, Spencer managed to escape when the Battle of Shiloh began. He arrived at the headquarters of Maj. Gen. Ulysses S. Grant at Pittsburg Landing on the second morning of the bloody battle. Spencer allegedly gave the Union commander the information he had collected on Confederate fortifications particularly at Island Number Ten, Tiptonville, and Fort Pillow, Tennessee, all of which he also wrapped up in a report to Captain Porter dated April 8. He then penned a letter to his sister Kitty, reassuring her he was not a deserter and that he had spent the last two months “constantly in the most difficult and dangerous service.” In July, the Essex steamed downriver for Vicksburg where it took part in the initial damaging broadsides with the Confederate iron-clad Arkansas. Shortly thereafter, Spencer led forty men on a successful mission to sink a ferryboat resupplying Port Hudson, Louisiana. Unfortunately, on Aug. 15, 1862, just two days before his twentieth birthday, Spencer was captured by enemy guerrillas who accused him of deserting the Confederate army. For the next year, as he was moved from Vicksburg to the notorious Castle Thunder in Richmond, Spencer maintained he had never mustered into a Confederate unit so was not a deserter. As for the spying charge, he allowed that he had been “employed by my Government to do what I did.” Unfortunately, exchange efforts by officials as high as the Secretary of the Navy came to naught. On Sept. 23, 1863, he was indicted as a spy and sentenced to hang two days later. At the time, Spencer reportedly told his chaplain, “The risk I knew; the responsibility I took; I will not shirk from the result.” At the gallows, in front of a large crowd, he helped his executioners adjust the noose around his neck. Then, the 21-year-old of light complexion and deep blue eyes met his fate with fortitude and the words “I mean to die as becomes a man.” *** Article by Lori S. Stewart, USAICoE Command Historian. New issues of This Week in MI History are published each week. To report story errors, ask questions, request previous articles, or be added to our distribution list, please contact: TR-ICoE-Command-Historian@army.mil.

items.title: Experience PTA Day connects Hawaii Island community with Army mission
items.author: Selina Gentkowski
items.summary: More than 200 Hawaii Island residents attended Experience PTA Day at Pohakuloa Training Area on Sept. 17 to explore military readiness, career pathways and conservation initiatives. The annual open house featured interactive equipment displays, live firefighting demonstrations and exhibits highlighting key community partnerships across the island. The event showcased how the garrison balances defense readiness with environmental stewardship and regional emergency support.
items.body:
POHAKULOA TRAINING AREA, Hawaii — Hawaii Island residents got a firsthand look at the people, programs and partnerships behind Pohakuloa Training Area during Experience PTA Day, an open house held Sept. 17.

The annual event welcomed community members from across the island to learn about military readiness, explore federal and civilian career opportunities and meet the personnel who support the installation’s mission. Attendees also had the opportunity to discover how PTA’s natural and cultural resource programs safeguard the land and native species while supporting vital military training.

“This event is for you, and we want you to ask questions, touch and feel the equipment, and learn about the many different aspects of PTA, including those that interface with the local community,” said Lt. Col. Paul Park, commander of U.S. Army Garrison Pohakuloa Training Area.

Park noted that more than 200 visitors attended the open house under clear skies to engage directly with service members and garrison staff.

During the event, natural and cultural resource personnel shared details about ongoing conservation efforts across tens of thousands of acres. These initiatives will soon operate under a new intergovernmental support agreement with local partners. For decades, subject-matter experts from Colorado State University and the University of Hawaii have supported the garrison’s cultural and environmental stewardship missions.

Soldiers from 2nd Battalion, 27th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Brigade Combat Team, 25th Infantry Division, presented a mortar system display, giving visitors a closer look at the weapon systems utilized during field exercises. Aviation personnel also participated, showcasing flight operations and the diverse units that routinely train at the high-elevation installation.

Demonstrations by the PTA Fire Department were a highlight for younger visitors, including a live demonstration of a high-capacity water cannon capable of discharging up to 3,000 gallons per minute.

“I really enjoyed the firefighters and their water cannon,” said one student after testing out a fire hose alongside emergency responders.

In addition to base demonstrations, the event featured booths and displays hosted by military recruiting services, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the U.S. Geological Survey, Kilauea Military Camp at Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, and Team Rubicon Waikoloa.

Visitors included students and faculty from Hilo High School, Connections Public Charter School and Waiakea High School, as well as representatives from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the Hawaii Division of Forestry and Wildlife.

Emergency services personnel also highlighted the installation’s vital mutual aid and regional safety role, including emergency medical responses along the Daniel K. Inouye Highway and collaborative wildland firefighting efforts with the Hawaii County Fire Department.

For community members familiar with PTA primarily through live-fire training exercises, Experience PTA Day offered a comprehensive look at the dedicated civilian and military personnel who sustain the garrison while balancing defense readiness with responsible stewardship.

items.body:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — Before sunrise, thousands began to climb.

They came from different communities, different universities, and different services. But at 6:30 a.m., inside Kenan Memorial Stadium, they all started moving in the same direction.

Up.

Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, more than 4,000 people gathered at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill to remember the first responders who climbed the stairs of the World Trade Center that morning.

Among them were firefighters, Raleigh police officers, and members of the North Carolina State Highway Patrol. Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC) cadets from UNC, Duke University, and North Carolina State University represented the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Air Force. Junior ROTC cadets joined veterans, civilians, and students who woke before dawn to take part.

Members of athletic teams across the university, including UNC head football coach Bill Belichick, traded fields, weight rooms, and water for the concrete steps of the stadium.

UNC, Duke, and NC State spend much of the year as rivals, but that morning, there was no competition. Only shared purpose.

Rivals Stand Together

Cadets and students from all three universities climbed the same stairs. They encouraged one another when the climb became difficult.

UNC Chancellor Lee H. Roberts, the university’s 13th chancellor and a graduate of Duke himself, joined Army Lt. Col. Lisa Klekowski, UNC’s Professor of Military Science, before the climb.

Together, Roberts addressed a generation of students who largely have no memory of the day they had gathered to commemorate.

For many of the participants, Sept. 11 is not a memory, it is history.

They did not watch a hijacked airliner disappear into the South Tower. They did not see smoke rise above Manhattan or watch the Pentagon burn. They did not experience the collective shock of a nation trying to understand what was happening that day.

Still, they climbed.

Inheriting the Future

After the attacks of Sept. 11 came two decades of war, deployments, and counterterrorism operations that fundamentally reshaped the U.S. military, the special operations community, and an entire generation of American service members.

The cadets climbing the stairs are inheriting the lessons of that generation, but they are not inheriting the same war.

Unmanned systems have changed the relationship between distance and danger. Electronic warfare can expose a position without a shot being fired. Inexpensive technology can destroy million-dollar pieces of equipment. Information moves around the globe in seconds. Technology is at the forefront of the next war.

But technology alone will not win it.

For the special operations community, this idea is not new. Today, one of the enduring Special Operations Forces truths may be more relevant than ever.

Humans Are More Important Than Hardware

Klekowski occupies an increasingly unique position between two generations.

Before UNC, she served as an aviator with the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment (Airborne) and later served within the U.S. Army Special Operations Command, part of the generation of Army leaders who spent much of their careers fighting the post-9/11 wars.

Now, Klekowski is responsible for passing on the hard-earned lessons of those years to help cadets on the battlefield, while instilling the leadership attributes required to win a war that looks completely different from the last.

Regardless of how technologically advanced the next war looks, when exhaustion, uncertainty, or fear take hold, someone has to be willing to take another step and convince the person beside them that they can take one too.

Carrying History Forward

As daylight slowly reached the stadium, legs grew heavy and breathing labored. Groups that started together began to stretch across the stadium's sections.

But everyone inside the stadium knew where the stairs would end. They knew they would eventually finish, and they knew their families would see them again.

The firefighters who entered the burning towers on September 11 had none of those assurances.

They climbed anyway.

items.title: Air Force Retires EC-130H, Embraces EA-37B, as Davis-Monthan Transitions
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: The 55th Wing officially retired the EC-130H Compass Call aircraft in a ceremony Sept. 18 at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz., while the 355th Wing there retired its final A-10 Warthog, another major transition for the base. The post Air Force Retires EC-130H, Embraces EA-37B, as Davis-Monthan Transitions appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The 55th Wing officially retired the EC-130H Compass Call aircraft in a ceremony Sept. 18 at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz., while the 355th Wing there inactivated its A-10 Warthog units, another major transition for the base.

The Compass Call mission is transitioning from the old propeller-driven EC-130s to the sleek EA-37B , which packs the electronic warfare mission into a modified Gulfstream 550 jet. The 55th Electronic Combat Group at Davis-Monthan has five of the new jets on hand, en route to a planned dozen by 2028 and 22 by 2031.

Meanwhile, the 355th is transitioning to a rescue mission as the base prepares to host a new special operations wing.

The new Compass Call jets compress the targeting, jamming, and other electronic warfare missions into a tighter space. About 70 percent of the equipment is unchanged, but instead of 13 Airmen performing Compass Call functions in the EC-130H, the E-37 B needs only nine.

“Its ‘plug-and-play’ architecture allows for rapid software updates and the integration of new capabilities to counter emerging threats and technologies without costly redesigns,” Maj. Claire Fitle, 355th Wing spokesperson, told Air & Space Forces Magazine by email.

The jet has “significantly increased speed, altitude, and range compared with the legacy EC-130H,” Fitle wrote. The equipment can also detect and jam a wider range of enemy systems from farther distances.

The new system is software-driven, allowing rapid updates via software rather than hardware modifications, “dramatically reducing response time … [to] evolving electromagnetic threats,” Fitle wrote.

Decade-long Road to Upgrade

The Air Force began seeking a replacement for the EC-130H in 2014, then awarded L3 Technologies a contract in 2017 to engineer the capability into a smaller airframe. Congress sped up the procurement program two years later, originally expecting to complete procurement in 2026.

The first five aircraft lack some low-band capability, which is anticipated in the remaining aircraft.

BAE Systems and L3Harris delivered the first EA-37B for developmental testing in 2023 , and Air Combat Command received the first two airframes in 2024 . Initial training sorties began in 2025 and operational testing wrapped up within the year. Contractors will be primarily responsible for maintaining the EA-37Bs at Davis-Monthan, Fitle wrote.

During Operation Epic Fury, they got their first combat exposure —even before the Air Force declared full operational capability.

The EC-130H saw combat action during Operation Just Cause in Panama, 1989, Operation Desert Storm in 1991, Operation Allied Force in Kosovo in 1999, and throughout the Global War on Terror in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Syria over the past 25 years. It was a workhorse to the end, making its final mission in the early stages of Operation Epic Fury.

The first legacy EC-130H retired in 2021, while the last aircraft conducted its final flight Sept. 2.

The 355th, 492nd, and the A-10

In a parallel event, the 355th inactivated its A-10 Warthog units as well Sept. 18. While the larger Air Force is keeping the popular close air support platform around until the 2030s, the 355th is becoming a “rescue hub,” Fitle wrote.

“Close air support is an enduring mission rather than a single airframe, and the Air Force will continue providing responsive CAS across the joint battlespace through a flexible mix of fifth- and fourth-generation multirole aircraft,” she wrote. “Experienced A-10 aircrew and maintainers are transitioning their close-support expertise directly into these platforms to ensure seamless coverage.”

The wing will continue its CSAR and personnel recovery mission through the 563rd Rescue Group using the HH-60W Jolly Green II helicopter and the HC-130J Combat King II aircraft.

Meanwhile, the 492nd Special Operations Wing is moving to Davis-Monthan, with full operational capability expected between 2028-29. The move comes as the USAF has restructured the former training wing.

The special ops wing will backfill the 355th’s A-10 capabilities by basing its OA-1K Skyraider II and CV-22 Osprey s at Davis-Monthan as well, expanding strike and specialized operational capabilities.

The former “high-end” strike missions will be absorbed by fifth-generation aircraft across USAF.

items.title: Now Back in Uniform: At Least 134 Airmen, Guardians Who Refused COVID Vaccine
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: More than 130 Airmen and Guardians have returned to service after leaving the military rather than receive the COVID-19 vaccine. And more could follow, an Air Force official said. The post Now Back in Uniform: At Least 134 Airmen, Guardians Who Refused COVID Vaccine appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —More than 130 Airmen and Guardians have returned to service after leaving the military rather than receive the COVID-19 vaccine. And more could follow, an Air Force official said.

Speaking at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs Richard Anderson said that, as of Sept. 15, 137 individuals have applied for reinstatement so far, and 48 have been accepted. Another 86 have returned through the reaccession process, for a total of 134 service members have already rejoined the ranks.

The two routes back are distinct: Reinstatement is slower, requiring interested veterans to apply to the Air Force Board for Correction of Military Records. If successful, the payoff is they will be eligible for back pay and other benefits—offset by whatever they earned in civilian jobs while separated. Reaccession, which is faster, skips the board process but also does not include back pay. A third option is to go through reaccession and only then apply for reinstatement after they have rejoined the ranks.

The Air Force and Space Force involuntarily separated about 600 Airmen and Guardsians for refusing the COVID shot: then-Undersecretary of the Air Force Gina Ortiz Jones pegged the number at 610 in early 2023 , and the Air Force Review Boards Agency said it identified 595 cases in a review earlier this year.

But others chose to leave when their service commitment was up rather than be vaccinated, and they are eligible to rejoin as well. Thousands of Airmen and Guardians sought medical and religious exemptions and refused the mandatory shots in 2021 and 2022. But the number that left voluntarily before the mandate was lifted in early 2023 is unclear.

Since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the Pentagon has made a concerted effort to make good on a campaign promise to restore those to service who departed because of the mandate, which was ordered by then-Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin. Current Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in April 2025 that his department was “welcoming actively back those warriors of conscience.”

Since then, the Pentagon has extended the deadline for applying until April 2027, and has reduced the minimum service obligation for those returning from four years to two.

Anderson and his team have also taken steps to ease the process for those who wish to return. In August, they announced medical processing and board reviews would take place simultaneously to speed the reinstatement process, and they hired case managers to help those seeking to return to service.

“We now, I think, have stabilized criteria and expectations,” Anderson said. “We have done a very sustained comms program to tell the affected universe that they are welcome back and welcome to apply … and we’ll continue to to advertise very heavily to get worthy Airmen and Guardians back in uniform.”

According to statistics compiled by the Department of the Air Force in December 2022 , just before the COVID vaccine mandate was lifted by an act of Congress, 97.6 percent of the 490,000 members of the Active-Duty Air Force and Space Force, Air National Guard, and Air Force Reserve got fully vaccinated, leaving about 11,700 unvaccinated. The department noted approximately 1,080 religious and administration exemptions to the mandate at the time.

items.title: Pentagon Picks 2 Companies for Reconnaissance Satellite Demo
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Force and the Defense Innovation Unit have chosen two firms to demonstrate the ability of small satellites built with low-cost, commercial technology to track both friendly and adversary satellites in geosynchronous orbit. The post Pentagon Picks 2 Companies for Reconnaissance Satellite Demo appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Space Force and the Defense Innovation Unit have chosen two firms to demonstrate the ability of small satellites built with low-cost, commercial technology to track both friendly and adversary satellites in geosynchronous orbit.

Northrop Grumman and True Anomaly will build prototype satellites for DIU’s GEO High-Resolution Optical Space-Based Tactical Reconnaissance, or GHOST-R, program, the Pentagon technology accelerator announced Sept. 18 in a LinkedIn post. The work will feed into a broader, multibillion dollar Space Force initiative called RG-XX, with the goal to begin fielding a fleet of reconnaissance satellites by the end of the decade.

Col. Bryon McClain, acting portfolio acquisition executive for space combat power, said the Space Force is trying to “push the envelope” when it comes to both speed and affordability.

“This approach burns down technical risk, drives down lifecycle costs, and gets vital capability to the warfighter faster to ensure a more resilient architecture,” McClain said. “Successful prototypes will have a direct transition into the program of record.”

The Space Force in 2024 started talking about a lower-cost, commercial-based capability to augment its current fleet of Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program , or GSSAP, satellites. At the time, then-acting space acquisition executive Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy said the approach was partly motivated by a push from U.S. Space Command for more unclassified opportunities to partner with allies and industry.

It also aims to address two other SPACECOM needs: more maneuverable satellites and better space domain awareness to close gaps in its ability to characterize and track objects of concern in space. As recently as Sept. 16, Space Command Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting called for improved on-orbit targeting and tracking capabilities—and highlighted the fundamental role space domain awareness plays in the counterspace mission.

“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” Whiting said at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go.”

In April, the Space Force chose 14 companies to be part of an industry consortium called Andromeda, where they’ll compete for task orders worth up to $6.2 billion. That contract will include work for both the maneuverable RG-XX reconnaissance satellites and a separate fleet of surveillance satellites called SG-XX.

As part of GHOST-R, Northrop and True Anomaly’s satellites are expected to launch in 2028 and then perform a series of demonstrations to prove they can collect high-resolution imagery and conduct weekly observations of target satellites. If successful, those spacecraft would become operational RG-XX platforms by 2029.

In parallel, the firms must provide a plan for scaling their satellites to a full constellation that can track all publicly catalogued objects in GEO.

Northrop, the incumbent prime contractor for GSSAP, said in a press release that its design will incorporate its ESPASat-L platform—a high-rate production bus—as well as optical payloads built by a company called TRL 11 based in Irvine, Calif.

“This award expands the company’s role in commercial, low-cost, proliferated space systems and builds on the success of the Northrop Grumman-built Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program,” the company said.

In its own statement, True Anomaly said it will leverage is Jackal spacecraft as well as its Mosaic ground system for GHOST-R.

“Jackal and Mosaic were purpose-built for this mission, delivering superior maneuverability, sensing, and autonomy at a price point that enables scale without compromising performance,” CEO Even Rogers said.

True Anomaly recently showcased its maneuverable Jackal spacecraft as part of the Space Force’s Victus Haze responsive space mission. During the mission, Jackal has demonstrated the ability to approach a target—in this case a satellite built by Rocket Lab—capture an image of it, characterize it, and “engage in a space-to-space pursuit” of the vehicle, the company said in a July statement.

Meanwhile, DIU recently posted another space-related solicitation , this time focused on fostering AI tools that can help distinguish between friendly objects and threats. The project, perhaps complementary to GHOST-R, seeks software that can “ingest and fuse massive streams of multi-source data,” like satellite imagery, geospatial data, and live video.

“By automating advanced cross-data correlation, the architecture aims to uncover hidden patterns, complex operational relationships, and predictive threat behaviors far beyond the capabilities of human analysis alone,” the solicitation states.

The Space Force revealed this week that it has space control weapons on orbit, but the head of U.S. Space Command said the U.S. still has “a long way to go” in improving its ability to detect and target threats in the domain.

As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.

The Space Development Agency wants to wrap up its Tranche 1 launch campaign by the end of spring 2027, flying six more batches of satellites to build out its tracking and data transport constellations, according to Director Gurpartap Sandhoo.

NASA is pushing hard to get astronauts back to the moon by 2028—and the urgency is driven in no small part by the national security implications of doing so before China does, Administrator Jared Isaacman said Sept. 15.

The Space Force estimates about 10 percent of its programs will be impacted under a continuing resolution for the coming fiscal year, according to Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess.

Guardians are playing a critical role in U.S. operations against Iran, providing electronic warfare effects to stifle enemy air defense and communication systems and other space capabilities vital to the war effort, Gen. Douglas Schiess said in one of his first appearances since swearing in as Chief of Space Operations.

Sept. 14, 2026

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed Sept. 14 the Space Force has “space control weapons” on orbit today—the Pentagon’s most direct acknowledgement to date that the U.S. is operating offensive capabilities in space.

Sept. 12, 2026

General Stephen Whiting took command of U.S. Space Command in January 2024, and if customary three-year tenures hold, his tour would end in January 2027. The question now before the President and Senate is who should follow him? Whoever they choose, it has to be a Guardian—and so should every successor…

items.title: Guidance: MAA Recognition
items.summary: Recognition is the process used to evaluate other military aviation regulators and assess the potential to use their airworthiness outputs within MAA processes.
items.body:
The Recognition process provides a structured evidence base to support a judgement on the extent to which another military aviation regulator’s technical airworthiness outputs would be acceptable for use within the MAA Certification or Organisational Approvals processes.

Recognition, however, does not mean that the work of another military aviation regulator can be used in the UK’s Defence Air Environment without further analysis. Their work must still be understood and assessed by the relevant DE&S Delivery Team Type Airworthiness Authority, in consultation with the MAA , with any differences that present a risk identified and sentenced. Further information about the use of Recognition within MAA processes can be found in Regulatory Articles 1005 and 5810 .

Further details

To undertake Recognition with other military aviation regulators the MAA uses the European Military Airworthiness Document Recognition ( EMAD R ) process developed through the European Defence Agency ( EDA ). This process revolves around the analysis of the other military regulator’s Responses to the Military Authorities’ Recognition Questionset ( MARQ ). The MARQ is contained in Annex D of the EMAD R and is derived from the International Civil Aviation Organization’s Doc 9734 (Safety Oversight Manual) and Doc 9760 (Airworthiness Manual).

The EMAD R can be found on the EDA airworthiness webpage

Evaluation of the Responses to the MARQ enables the MAA to assess the scope of another military aviation regulator’s responsibilities and regulations in the following areas:

general functions of an airworthiness authority

airworthiness inspection regulations

production oversight regulations

aircraft certification regulations

Military aviation regulators can decide to conduct Recognition on a one-way or a two-way (ie mutual) basis, depending on the business need of the nations involved.

The EMAD R process is being used widely by military aviation regulators and it is also the basis for the Five Eyes Air Force Interoperability Council Recognition process and the NATO Recognition Process.

For further information please contact the MAA ’s International Engagement and Recognition Team via:

Email: DSA- MAA -MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk

items.title: How the Air Force Rigged F-15s in the Middle East with Drone-Busting Rockets in a Week
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: As the threat of Iranian-made drones grew, the Air Force rushed last year to equip F-15E Strike Eagles in the Middle East with a cheap, cost-effective way of defeating them. The service fielded the new capability in roughly a week. The post How the Air Force Rigged F-15s in the Middle East with Drone-Busting Rockets in a Week appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.— As the threat of Iranian-made drones rose in recent conflicts, the Air Force rushed last year to equip F-15E Strike Eagle s in the Middle East with a cheap, cost-effective way of defeating them.

The Air Force Test Center was able to field the new capability—laser-guided rockets—in roughly a week, the head of the center revealed at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference here Sept. 16.

It’s not the first time the Air Force has turned to this solution, known as the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, to neutralize enemy one-way attack drones and cruise missiles.

APKWS was originally designed as an air-to-ground capability, with a laser-guided kit added to Hydra-70 rockets to turn the system into a precision-guided munition.

The Air Force explored using the rockets in an air-to-air role in 2019, testing the system on the F-16 Fighting Falcon . For a few years, the experiment was considered nothing more than a proof of concept, not a real-world capability.

But as the use of Iranian drones was expanded, the program gained new urgency. The system was rushed first to F-16s in 2024 and then prioritized for F-15Es in 2025. Nine days after testing began in May of last year, the system was being equipped on Strike Eagles overseas, said Brig. Gen. Mark A. Massaro.

“At the end of the first week, we had demonstrated, both in a developmental and an operational sense, that it was a usable capability, and we deployed that capability at the end of the first week,” Massaro said. “We deployed that capability into theater. We deployed some of our maintainers and some of our testers into theater to help the first week.”

The initiative is an example of the Air Force Test Center’s ability to quickly “bridge between raw concept and decisive combat-credible power,” said Massaro. He was involved in tests of APKWS in his previous role as commander of the 96th Test Wing, which conducts developmental testing of weapons for the service, and worked alongside the 53rd Wing, which conducts operational tests.

The need for the system was clear. The Air Force had relied on expensive, radar-guided AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles and infrared-guided AIM-9 Sidewinders against Tehran’s relatively cheap Shahed one-way attack drones. AMRAAMs cost roughly $1 million each, and AIM-9s cost hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on the variant. The most capable model is the AIM-9X, which costs around $500,000.

The issue came to a head with a mass Iranian drone and ballistic missile attack aimed at Israel on April 13, 2024. Tehran, which sought to flood the zone, launched a barrage of drones, ballistic missiles, and cruise missiles to confuse and overwhelm Israel’s air defenses—some 300 projectiles in all.

The U.S. had anticipated the engagement, and F-15Es from the 335th Fighter Squadron and 494th Fighter Squadron carried up to eight air-to-air missiles each as they sought to intercept the drones over Iraq along with F-16s from the 121st Fighter Squadron. The Iranian drone barrage was so heavy that many fighters quickly exhausted their air-to-air missiles, and three F-15E crews attempted—unsuccessfully—to drop laser-guided JDAM bombs on drones.

While U.S. fighters had helped to defeat the barrage, it was an expensive proposition, which led to the effort to adapt APKWS rockets, which cost roughly $35,000 according to Air Force officials.

Dubbed the AGR-20F FALCO, the air-to-air APKWS rockets were first used in an air-to-air configuration on F-16s in 2024.

After that, work began at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., to equip the system on F-15Es. That occurred in mid-2025, led by 96th Wing’s Air Force Seek Eagle Office, known as AFSEO, which had earlier integrated the system into F-16s.

“This was a very integrated test approach between operational and developmental,” Massaro said. “We were overlaying … missions on exactly the same day with each other and flying them together. That second week, where we have our maintainers and some pilots in theater, our operational testers are still refining some of the tactics, and we’re able to then through phone and digital means transmit the upgraded tactics. And then, so at the end of that second week, they had updated tactics, they had equipment, they had everything ready to go, and they were able to use it very quickly after that.”

Early last year, the team initially struggled to find a way to mount the rockets on the F-15E and connect them to the aircraft so they could be fired. In May 2025, a solution was found, and the integration became the top priority for the 96th Test Wing and 53rd Wing at the base, according to Air Force officials.

Aircrew from the 40th Flight Test Squadron and the 85th and 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadrons flew test missions and conducted live-fire tests at targets over land and water.

After the initial demonstrations, the 53rd Wing and 96th Test Wing deployed to deliver equipment and provide training to Airmen to use the new weapons. While the Air Force has declined to identify the location where the system was first fielded, U.S. officials confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that air-to-air APKWS was first used in the Middle East, which is part of U.S. Central Command.

In 2024, Air Forces Central began to equip its F-16s to shoot down drones in the Middle East with APKWS rockets, which were employed to defeat threats from the Houthis in Yemen .

A U.S. F-16 scored its first rocket kill of a drone that year. In October 2024, the 480th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron from Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, deployed to the Middle East with an advance but limited heads-up that they would be equipped with APKWS for air-to-air use against drones and cruise missiles.

“The first rocket kill was announced just prior to getting there. This was all new and innovative,” Lt. Col. William “Skate” Parks, the unit’s commander, recounted in a December 2025 interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “We have these rockets come online. It’s a brand new thing, and we’re the ones doing it. And it’s with guys who are now spending every minute of their day when they’re not flying actual combat missions, preparing and improving on this. It showed because that success rate just started really becoming amazing with these rockets as we’re defending partners and our own forces.”

The 480th scored dozens of kills using the rockets . It also used older AIM-9M Sidewinders, claiming the first air-to-air kill by an AIM-9M in over 30 years, and 108 total aerial kills of drones and cruise missiles during the deployment. News of the success quickly trickled across the Air Force.

By April 2025, U.S. Air Forces in Europe incorporated the APKWS into its air-to-air training for F-16s , Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported. U.S. fighters based on the continent not only routinely deploy to the Middle East, but also increasingly must be wary of Russian drone incursions into NATO airspace. The F-16 experience helped speed up the use of the APKWS as a drone-buster on the F-15E, Massaro said.

“A lot of things had already occurred,” he said. “The F-16 had already integrated APKWS and was flying with that for about a year, so we knew how the system itself worked. We had that knowledge. The F-15E is a known quantity.”

APKWS rockets come in pods of seven, and multiple rocket pods can be fitted. F-15Es can carry up to 42 APKWS rockets. To guide an APKWS rocket, the target must be laser-designated or “lased,” unlike more expensive “fire-and-forget” missiles. This means air-to-air use of the rocket pods is best suited to defeating slow-flying targets such as one-way attack drones.

The work to put APKWS on the F-16 and F-15E would pay off in more than just cost savings for the Air Force. After the start of Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, Iran has fired more than 6,000 drones and 1,500 ballistic missiles, with numbers growing, U.S. officials said. What two years ago was an extreme outlier is now a routine threat.

F-16s flying in the area around the Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf, and Gulf of Oman, where Iran has repeatedly used drones and missiles to attack ships including U.S. Navy vessels, are flying with APKWS rocket pods to hunt down drones. U.S. Army Apache helicopters can also fire APKWS rockets in an air-to-air role , another recent capability fielded by the military. The U.S. also needs to protect its bases in the Middle East.

The former head of Air Forces Central, Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, said the use of APKWS was a key development during his tenure , which ended last month.

“From a technical aspect, it’s ‘Hey, I need more weapons on my jet,’ and that’s what the APKWS gives you: a pod of seven of those things versus a single AIM-9. You can shoot down a lot more drones when they’re coming in swarms,” France said in a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “From an operational perspective, there’s not just the magazine depth of an individual airplane, which I care about, but I care about the magazine depth of the theater and making sure that, across the theater, I’ve got wings with the right weapons in the right place and get them in the air where they can defend their bases. … There’s the cost curve, which is significant as well.”

And the proliferation of the drone threat is only increasing, U.S. military officials and experts say, making further advancements necessary.

“I would say that APKWS is a step in the right direction, but it can’t be the final step,” France said. “The two things that we need to focus on are air domain awareness at range: where are the drones coming from? How many are there? What’s their target? What do I know about them? And then magazine depth, both individual airplanes and theater-wise, to have enough to shoot them down in a layered defense kind of way. So both of those are important.”

“This drone problem is not going away. It’s accelerating in tactics, speed, advancements, and the numbers,” France added. “That’s the direction that we’re going.”

Air Force depots are not typically meant for quick repair jobs, but during Operation Epic Fury, the service moved some of its stateside heavy maintenance capability forward to fix battle-damaged aircraft closer to the fight.

The 55th Wing officially retired the EC-130H Compass Call aircraft in a ceremony Sept. 18 at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz., while the 355th Wing there retired its final A-10 Warthog, another major transition for the base.

More than 130 Airmen and Guardians have returned to service after leaving the military rather than receive the COVID-19 vaccine. And more could follow, an Air Force official said.

Sept. 17, 2026

An F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing crashed during a training mission in Michigan on Sept. 17. The fighter's sole pilot ejected and is in stable condition at a local hospital.

When Space Force leaders started talking about expanding the service early this year, the idea was simple: double the size of the force in the next five years. At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, officials detailed just how they’re planning to grow so much so quickly.

The Air Force’s new Collaborative Combat Aircraft will take part in their first large-force engagement exercise in December, the head of the drones’ Experimental Operations Unit said Sept. 15.

The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters.

Sept. 16, 2026

As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.

Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.

Military low flying: RAF operational low flying training timetable

Royal Air Force (RAF) operational low flying training timetables in 3 areas of the UK.

From:

Ministry of Defence

Published:

1 August 2011

Last updated:

18 September 2026 — See all updates

Documents

Operational Low Flying Training Timetable 14 to 18 September 2026

HTML

Operational Low Flying Training Timetable 21 September to 25 September 2026

Operational Low Flying Training Timetable 28 September to 2 October 2026

Details

Timetables for operational low flying ( OLF ) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas ( TTA ) only. These are:

LFA 7(T): central Wales

LFA 14(T): northern Scotland

LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England

When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.

Other low flying schedules

Military low flying: MOD sponsored air exercises

Military low flying: air weapons ranges activity

Related information

Low flying military aircraft includes information about how to contact MOD about low flying in your area

Military low flying includes detailed information about why we carry out low flying in the UK

items.title: Housing reforms give military families greater say over their homes
items.summary: Military families will have a greater say over the homes they live in under a package of reforms designed to cut bureaucracy, strengthen accountability and put residents at the heart of housing services.
items.body:
A new Red Tape Challenge, announced today by the Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, will invite military families to identify and remove outdated housing rules, while new national and regional committees will ensure their experiences directly influence future decisions about accommodation services and a ground-breaking pilot will give them a role in signing off repairs to their homes.

The measures build on recent changes already introduced by the Ministry of Defence, including ending outdated restrictions on keeping pets and giving families greater freedom to decorate their homes.

They form part of the Government’s £9.2 billion Defence Housing Strategy, which will transform military housing through the new Defence Housing Service, delivering better homes, improved service standards and a stronger focus on the needs of Service personnel and their families.

Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting MP, said:

Service families should not feel that decisions about their homes are being made without them. These reforms are about giving families more power and control, with a stronger voice in shaping housing services and a clear route to challenge things that aren’t working. Alongside major investment in defence housing, we are determined to build a service that listens and delivers the standard of housing our Armed Forces and their families deserve.

Service families should not feel that decisions about their homes are being made without them. These reforms are about giving families more power and control, with a stronger voice in shaping housing services and a clear route to challenge things that aren’t working.

Alongside major investment in defence housing, we are determined to build a service that listens and delivers the standard of housing our Armed Forces and their families deserve.

A new Code of Conduct will ensure families receive a more consistent and respectful service from everyone representing Defence housing, including contractors across the supply chain.

A new pilot is also being introduced that will give families a greater role in signing off repairs and maintenance work, helping to ensure issues are fully resolved and work is completed to the expected standard before jobs are closed.

A new Customer Committee will also give families a direct voice in decision-making at a national level, while Regional Experience Committees will bring together residents from across the country to identify local issues and help shape future services. Together, the committees will ensure that family feedback informs decisions across the Defence housing system. This shows the government’s commitment to problem-solving and putting power back into local communities.

Tricia Jakeman, Defence Families Champion, whose role it is to listen to Service families and the challenges they are facing, said:

Behind every military home is a family whose support is essential to operational life. Giving Service families a stronger voice in the decisions that affect them is not only the right thing to do, it is essential if we are to deliver the quality of housing and services they deserve. The changes we’ve seen over the past year show what can be achieved when families are listened to, and this is an important step in ensuring their voices continue to drive positive change.

Behind every military home is a family whose support is essential to operational life. Giving Service families a stronger voice in the decisions that affect them is not only the right thing to do, it is essential if we are to deliver the quality of housing and services they deserve.

The changes we’ve seen over the past year show what can be achieved when families are listened to, and this is an important step in ensuring their voices continue to drive positive change.

The Defence Housing Strategy, launched in November, set out the MOD’s plans to reform military housing over the next decade. Backed by £9.2 billion of investment, it will be delivered through the Defence Housing Service, which will be formally established in April 2027.

Service families can find out more about the Red Tape Challenge and submit their suggestions here: Red Tape Challenge

items.title: A Design Lab Pilot to Inform Strategies for Expanding Access to Medications for Opioid Use Disorder in Community Mental Health Centers
items.author: Bradley D. Stein
items.summary: A pilot Design Lab identified barriers and strategies to improving access to medications for opioid use disorder in community mental health settings. Expanding insurer reimbursement via a learning exchange was seen as most impactful and feasible.
items.body:
Allison J. Ober , Sarah B. Hunter , Alex R. Dopp , Bradley D. Stein

Research Published Sep 18, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

This pilot Design Lab engaged clients, clinic leaders, and policy experts to identify barriers and strategies for expanding access to medications for opioid use disorder. Stigma, workforce shortages, regulatory complexity, and payment limitations emerged as key challenges. Expanding insurer reimbursement through a structured learning exchange was rated highest in impact and feasibility, suggesting cross-sector collaboration may advance access.

Guidance for new suppliers

A common way for suppliers to bid for contracts is via online platforms known as frameworks. These are usually set up to help government buy a specific type of product or service, and have standard terms and processes which make it easier to contract with us. Once you are on a framework you can apply for any advertised opportunities until the framework ends.

Each challenge is set over a period of 12-16 weeks. HMGCC will work closely with applicants and offering funding and expertise. The contracting times are short, and suppliers will still own their IP, and will be supported in driving early concept closer to becoming real world solution.
